expect:
All relevant and accurate points should be credited.
Top band (13-16): Complex explanation of stated factor and other factor(s) leading to a sustained judgement. Answer demonstrates a range of accurate and detailed knowledge and understanding. Complex, sustained line of reasoning which is sharply focused and fully substantiated. Students move from developed explanation by complex explanation of the relationship between causes to form a sustained judgement.
Example: The USA’s absence was the single most damaging factor because it weakened the League in three interconnected ways. Economically, sanctions were useless since the world’s richest nation could keep trading with aggressors. Militarily, the League could not call on America’s huge army. Politically, it was Wilson’s creation yet his own country refused to join, meaning no one truly wanted to lead. However, even with the USA the League’s structural flaws would have limited its effectiveness. The unanimity requirement, veto power, and no standing army meant decisive action was almost impossible by design. Both the absent USA and the flawed structure worked together to cripple the League.

Example (stated factor): The USA’s absence was hugely damaging because it weakened sanctions. Wilson lost the 1920 election to Harding, who adopted isolationism. Many Americans opposed joining because they did not want to be dragged into foreign wars.

The Council’s permanent members had veto power, allowing self-interested nations to protect themselves or their allies. The Permanent Court at The Hague had no way to enforce its rulings.

Example: America did not join the League so sanctions did not work. / The League had no army.

All relevant and accurate points should be credited.
Top band (7-8): Complex analysis of causation/consequence. Answer is presented in a coherent narrative/account that demonstrates a range of accurate and detailed knowledge and understanding. Students move from a developed narrative with complex sequencing and reasoning, showing understanding of HOW/WHY events in Abyssinia destroyed the League.
Example: The events showed the League was openly sabotaged by the actions of leading member nations. Italy, a permanent Council member, invaded Abyssinia in October 1935 using tanks, aircraft, and poison gas. The League imposed economic sanctions but deliberately excluded oil, coal, and steel — the very resources Italy needed for war — and left the Suez Canal open. The League was further undermined by the secret Hoare-Laval Pact (December 1935), in which Britain and France tried to give Mussolini two-thirds of Abyssinia. This showed that self-interest was their priority; they wanted to keep Mussolini on their side rather than Hitler’s. When the pact was leaked, both ministers were forced to resign, but the damage to the League’s credibility was irreversible. Italy conquered Abyssinia in May 1936 and left the League.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Developed analysis of causation/consequence. Answer is presented in a structured and well-ordered narrative/account with a range of accurate knowledge. Shows analysis of how/why at one stage.
Example: Mussolini’s invasion of Abyssinia showed that the League lacked the strength to prevent acts of aggression because the only way it could have any influence was by imposing trade sanctions. However, the sanctions against Italy in 1935–36 did not include oil, coal, or steel, so Mussolini’s military capability was not compromised. Britain also refused to close the Suez Canal, the main route for Italian supply ships, because it feared this would push Mussolini towards an alliance with Hitler.

Example: Italy invaded Abyssinia in October 1935 and the League imposed sanctions. But the sanctions did not include oil or coal. The Hoare-Laval Pact was a secret deal that tried to give Italy most of Abyssinia. Italy conquered Abyssinia in May 1936 and then left the League.
Lower band (1-2): Basic analysis of causation/consequence. General statements with basic knowledge.
Example: Italy invaded Abyssinia and the League could not stop it. / The sanctions were too weak to make a difference.
0 marks: No evidence or fails to address the question.
